newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli forex market still in flux.
newsitem.headline: Israeli forex market still in flux.

text.p: Israel's shekel took a dive on Monday, weighed down by what traders said was an atmosphere of uncertainty in the wake of last week's foreign exchange reforms.

The representative rate for the dollar was fixed at 3.4840 shekels against 3.4370 on Friday. The basket, composed of the dollar, mark, pound sterling, French franc and yen, was fixed at 3.7869 against 3.7345 on Friday.

The resignation of Finance Minister Dan Meridor in protest at some of the reforms and the likelihood Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon, a champion of Jewish settlements, would succeed him, had little direct impact on the currency market.
Traders said it was a matter of technicalities rather than personalities.

"Companies sold dollars last week on expectations of the shekel's appreciation as the government was expected to approve the widening of the trading band," said a dealer at United Mizrahi Bank. "Now they are trying to cut the losses."
The government approved foreign exchange reforms on Wednesday but left the lower limit of the basket unchanged, erasing any possibility of the shekel's appreciation.
The Mizrahi trader said another reason for the shekel's drop was that banks were closing short positions.
"The Bank of Israel cleaned out the market on Tuesday (buying close to $500 million) and now there are not enough dollars in the market and banks and companies have to cover themselves," he said.
On the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, shares closed mixed in volatile trading after recovering from early losses in response to the shekel's sharp drop against the dollar, traders said.

The benchmark Mishtanim index of the top 100 shares ended down 0.19 percent, or 0.56 points, to 296.35 on all-share turnover of 229 million shekels against 265 million shekels on Sunday. The Maof 25 blue chip index closed 0.21 percent higher at 304.69.

Meanwhile, markets will be avidly following a vote of no-confidence in parliament on Tuesday which, barring any last-minute surprises, the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is expected to win.

It remained to be seen however how many of the coalition members who make up Netanyahu's 66-54 majority would embarrass him and abstain as an expression of their disaffection with the way he runs the government.
Little more than a year into office, Netanyahu has come under pressure from coalition members demanding help for constituents and control of ministries he was due to dish out in a cabinet reshuffle.
"We have a government which will continue. The coalition is stable. There are problems -- they'll be solved," Netanyahu said on Monday.
